content: The Surveillance Guide for Vaccine-Preventable Diseases in the WHO South-East Asia Region, Module 3: Poliomyelitis was published in September 2023 by the World Health Organization (WHO). This document provides detailed guidance on the surveillance of poliomyelitis, a vaccine-preventable disease, in the South-East Asia region. The guide outlines the objectives and methods of poliomyelitis surveillance, which is critical for global polio eradication efforts. The South-East Asia region was declared free of wild poliovirus types 1, 2, and 3 in 2014. However, as of 2022, wild poliovirus type 1 (WPV1) remains endemic in Afghanistan and Pakistan, posing a risk of importation to the region. Additionally, circulating vaccine-derived polioviruses (cVDPVs) present a risk of outbreaks. High-quality surveillance is essential for the timely detection of WPV and VDPV transmission, as well as the circulation of Sabin-like viruses. The guide describes three main components of poliovirus surveillance: acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance, environmental surveillance (ES), and surveillance among patients with primary immunodeficiency disorders (PIDs). These efforts are supported by the Global Poliovirus Laboratory Network (GPLN) and the comprehensive Polio Information System, which provide access to data for informed decision-making. AFP surveillance is the cornerstone of polio eradication efforts and is considered the gold standard for detecting poliovirus circulation. Countries must be able to identify suspected AFP cases through active surveillance, passive surveillance, or community-based surveillance. AFP surveillance should ideally be linked with other surveillance systems, such as case-based surveillance for measles-rubella and integrated surveillance for other vaccine-preventable or outbreak-prone diseases. Countries conducting immunodeficiency-related VDPV surveillance, enterovirus surveillance, or ES for polio should also integrate AFP surveillance with these efforts. A suspected AFP case is defined as any child under 15 years of age presenting with sudden onset of floppy paralysis or muscle weakness due to any cause, or any person of any age with paralytic illness if poliomyelitis is suspected by a physician. The date of onset of paralysis is considered the date of onset of AFP. All suspected cases must be investigated within 48 hours of notification by trained health staff or clinicians designated by public health authorities. Since polio can be difficult to differentiate from other forms of AFP (e.g., Guillain-Barré syndrome, transverse myelitis, or traumatic neuritis), all children with AFP should be reported and tested for poliovirus, even if clinical grounds suggest otherwise. A standard case investigation form should be used to document relevant information about the suspected case, including demographics, clinical features, neurological examination findings, medical and travel history, vaccination status, and risk factors. It is important to determine whether the suspected case traveled outside their area of residence or received visitors from outside the area within 35 days prior to the onset of paralysis. Exposure to anyone with AFP during this period should also be assessed. Each AFP case must be assigned a unique case identification number, also known as an epidemiological number (EPID number), which includes a geographical location code, the year of onset, and a serial case number. This number should be cited in all communications and forms related to the case. Testing for poliovirus involves analyzing stool specimens for the presence of the virus. Adequate stool specimens must be collected as soon as possible after the onset of paralysis, ideally within 14 days. Two specimens, collected at least 24 hours apart, are required. The highest concentration of poliovirus in stool occurs during the first two weeks after paralysis onset. If specimens cannot be collected within 14 days, they should be collected up to 60 days after onset. Specimens must be sealed in containers, stored at 4–8°C in a cold box, and transported to a laboratory within 72 hours. If this is not possible, specimens should be frozen at -20°C and shipped frozen, ideally with dry ice or cold packs, following the reverse cold chain procedures. A laboratory request form must be completed for each case, and the EPID number should be recorded on the specimen container and form. Specimens should be sent using the fastest and most reliable transport method available, and expertise is required for packaging and documentation compliant with International Air Transport Association (IATA) regulations. In critically ill children unable to pass stool, rectal tube samples may be collected, though the volume may be insufficient for additional testing, and virus isolation rates may be lower. Adequate stool specimens are defined as two specimens collected within 14 days of paralysis onset, at least 24 hours apart, with each specimen being 8–10 grams in volume and arriving at a WHO-accredited laboratory in good condition. Good condition means no desiccation or leakage, with proper documentation and evidence of cold chain maintenance. Contact sampling involves collecting and testing one stool specimen from three individuals in contact with an AFP case. This method provides laboratory evidence of poliovirus in an AFP case and helps confirm poliovirus infection in cases not otherwise laboratory-confirmed. Contacts are individuals who have had close interaction (e.g., touching, sharing toys, or food) with an AFP case.
